subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO NETHERLANDS LOAN ADVANCE REPAYMENT

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO NETHERLANDS LOAN ADVANCE REPAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this statement would have been given on Friday had I received official notification of it in time to give it on the order for motions. As a matter of courtesy I am making it now.
As the house undoubtedly knows at this time, the government of the Netherlands paid to the government of Canada in advance of maturity $32,130,000, representing one half of the remaining debt owed by the Netherlands to Canada for credits received in the years immediately following world war II.
The credits to the Netherlands were part of the post-war Canadian program of assistance to many European countries, including the United Kingdom, Belgium, France, the Netherlands and Norway, designed to help in the reconstruction of their economies. The total credits extended by Canada to the Netherlands in the immediate post-war period amounted to $123.9 million. Repayments by the Netherlands to the end of April, 1962 had reduced the amount outstanding to $64,260,000.
The Canadian government has welcomed this initiative of the Netherlands government. The repayment of this sum in advance constitutes impressive evidence of the economic progress achieved by the Netherlands since 1947; it is a further example of the close ties of friendship between Canada and the Netherlands, and of the growing economic co-operation among the free nations of the world. It will make a further substantial contribution toward the strengthening of Canada's foreign exchange position.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first session of this new parliament is but a few days old and it already seems as though it is going to be a long one, profitable for the Canadian people, yet deceiving for the opposition.
I should like to associate myself with the distinguished members who spoke before me, to offer my humble congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. members for Waterloo South (Mr. Chaplin) and for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent). Last fall, I made discreet inquiries in Nicolet-Yamaska to find a worthy replacement for His Excellency Hon. Paul Comtois, lieutenant governor of the province of Quebec, who had resigned his seat. Today, I am glad that last June 18, the people of that constituency approved the wise choice I made. I congratulate not only the new member for Nicolet-Yamaska but all the people of that fine riding for having elected a true farmer, a young man who will, in the true tradition of the Conservative party, uphold the rights of the Quebec farmers who were too long ignored by the Liberals at both the provincial and federal levels.
Speaking of new members, I should like to take this opportunity to offer my congratulations and encouragement to a member of the opposition, the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pilon), whose grandfather, Dr. Hormidas Pilon, a professional veterinarian, represented the provincial riding of Vaudreuil at the Quebec legislative assembly for 32 years. He was a friend of the farmers, and the latter showed him eternal gratitude for the countless services he rendered to them. I hope the hon. member will follow in his grandfather's footsteps. He can be sure of my wholehearted sympathy when he has to discuss agriculture within the Liberal caucus or take the advice or orders of the turncoat member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), the Liberal expert on agriculture.
With regard to farming, I would like to draw a parallel between recent Liberal policy in this field and the principles applied by the Conservatives in the county I represent.
On one occasion-in 1940, if I remember correctly, and under Liberal rule-a unit of bulldozers invaded St. Dominique and St. Fereol in Vaudreuil-Soulanges, tearing down fences, toppling down trees, filling in ditches and letting the cattle of about 40 farmers and milk producers run off in an undescrib-able scramble before an invasion ordered by the dictators of this century, the Liberals of Ottawa.
In order to win the war and annihilate the common enemy, the farmers' fields and herds, as well as the observance of ownership rights, had lost their significance: those peaceful

The Address-Mr. Bourbonnais people had to be shown that Canada was at war and that not even a second could be lost to build storehouses for explosives.
The administration of the day did not think it fit to send a message of warning to the farmers of that area to enable them to put their cattle on some other pasture, before the contractors' equipment changed the site earmarked by the Liberal high command for the erection of storage space for explosive matter.
You may imagine the disappointment, not to say the disgust, Mr. Speaker, felt by those 40 farmers or so who saw their land being invaded, their cattle chased about and their crops ruined because instructions had been given by the political appointees of the Liberal government to disregard ownership rights: the war effort was to be a total one, the stocking of explosive matters had a priority over the protection of cattle and farmers' rights.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a factual illustration of the Liberal attitude with regard to the farmers of Vaudreuil-Soulanges.
Moreover, after seizing part of their land for which a derisive price had been arbitrarily set, the Department of Defence Production under Liberal rule registered some assessments for about 75 per cent of the whole acreage included while offering $1 a year per acre in compensation. Not only did those farmers have their cattle annihilated, their crops and land put to waste, but they also had to suffer a considerable devaluation of their property without receiving-and this was under Liberal rule-any compensation from the Department of Defence Production.
For over 18 years of Liberal rule in the county of Vaudreuil-Soulanges, these forty-odd farmers had to endure the oppression of their Liberal dictators who, every time these farmers dared complain, would reply: "There is the solution, take it or leave it!"
A Conservative government had to come along, which studied the farmer's problems and offered them a more equitable compensation, which was accepted.
Today that problem is settled, and those farmers are happy to have received double the offer of the Liberals, thanks to the understanding and the intelligent policies of the present Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley) to whom I wish to express my sincere gratitude on behalf of the people whom I have the honour to represent here.


This, Mr. Speaker, proves the positive arrogance with which the Liberals approached agricultural problems in Vaudreuil-Soulanges.
Again today the farmers in my county are being pushed around by another Liberal government. This time, it is the construction of the trans-Canada highway to which the federal government contributes generously. Under the federal statute enacted in that respect, the location of the highway and the expropriation of land come under the exclusive jurisdiction of the province. The locations chosen by the provincial Liberal government could not make less sense. In Vaudreuil-Soulanges, the highway seems to have been designed so as to destroy as many cultivated areas as possible, thus forcing many farmers to abandon their farms. When the actual construction starts, the Liberals use the same system which is dear to them. Graders start working on the fields, destroying fences, wells and crops, without the owners being advised even a few hours in advance.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals' attitude towards farmers never changes. They seem to enjoy harassing the farmers. I should like to give another example of their lack of consideration for those people whose properties are expropriated to make way for the trans-Canada highway. Lately, a minister in Mr. Lesage's cabinet compelled a school board to buy land at $5,000 an acre for the construction of high schools. This land forms part of a 400-acre farm bought at $1,000 an acre by a group of Liberals under the instructions of the Liberal minister. It is adjacent to the land which will be expropriated for the trans-Canada highway. But the Quebec Liberal government has offered the farmers $250 an acre only for the land to be expropriated. The farmers are given $250 while friends of the Liberal party receive $1,000.
This is a further proof of the lack of consideration, to say the least, that the provincial Liberals as well as the federal Liberals have for the farmers.
When friends or institutions founded by them are concerned, the Liberals are ready to pay a high price; but they do not have the decency to give proper compensation to farmers who are deprived of their property.
There is another case which clearly shows the lack of seriousness of provincial Liberals,

caused by the paltry directives given by the federal member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), and in order to better identify him, I mean the ex-member for Stormont, who has now been transferred to the leadership of the federal Liberals in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, this house will remember the pressure-

In support of his friends, who were about to vanish from the Quebec political picture, and making himself their spokesman, the hon. member for Laurier was preaching the importance of providing for the welfare of birds and fish, instead of supporting our project of a more practical use of the Soulanges canal properties, that is the sale of certain parts of the canal to interested firms, in order that some manufacturing industries

But, since then, the friends of the hon. member for Laurier have kept silent, have not yet accepted the federal government's offer of handing over to them all properties in the Soulanges canal area, valued at more than $200,000, for the "enormous" sum of $1. They prepared a model at great cost and displayed huge descriptive panels of their project at the sportmen's show held in the trade mart in Montreal. The minister of game and fisheries, accompanied by his deputy minister, his secretary, the director of fish-breeding for the province of Quebec, his assistant, the chief engineer of highways and his assistant, all of them came here last March in order to urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) to transfer the canal to them immediately. They were even generous enough to give him 15 days to make a decision. This entire delegation, which was typically Liberal, made the trip from Quebec city to Ottawa at great cost, to demand that the Soulanges canal be handed over entirely to the Quebec Liberal government. They insisted that a decision be taken without delay so that fish could be put in the canal to enable fishermen to practise their favourite sport early in the following season.
On July 7, 1961, the Minister of Transport stated in this house that he was willing to

The Address-Mr. Bourbonnais transfer the Soulanges canal to the Quebec Liberal government at the ridiculously low price of $1, and the minister of game and fisheries expressed his satisfaction at this happy solution, as reported in the press. But since that time, that is over a period of 15 months, we have not yet heard from the Liberal government of Quebec, nor from the minister of game and fisheries and we got no reply. Apparently, the ministers of the Lesage cabinet are too busy unravelling the threads of the Shawinigan water and power matter to follow up the projects about which they were raising such a clamour last year. I wonder what the hon. member for Laurier will have to say concerning the Soulanges canal.
Talking about the former member for Stormont, I must congratulate him for having the new member for this constituency elected.
But, Mr. Speaker, do you know how he realized that feat? It was because the hon. member for Laurier talked at only one meeting held by the Liberal candidate.

Turning to other matters, Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw the government's attention to the question of taxes paid to the federal government by companies producing power for public consumption.
It is urgent for the federal government to amend the Income Tax Act as regards corporations so that such provinces where power systems are privately owned may collect all taxes which power companies pay to the federal treasury. Such provinces would then be placed on an equal footing with those which own the power systems and, therefore, do not pay federal taxes.
This anomaly has become one of the main arguments used by a few socialists who have


forced their way into Quebec's provincial Liberal party and who, through their revolutionary cries, are seeking to divide the French-speaking and English-speaking elements of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, as I do not believe in state ownership, I am against the nationalization of power companies-which Quebec's Liberal party wants to bring about-because in the long run, an enterprise without competition, that is without any counterpart in private enterprise, always ends up by costing more to. the taxpayer. Its employees, having lost all sense of efficiency, initiative and ambition, become slack and remiss in their work. Such an enterprise also tends to increase its personnel at an excessive rate, which makes for higher operating costs.
Mr. Speaker, if the Quebec hydro should take over all the power companies in Quebec and the management of all their personnels, we would then see the greatest network of patronage ever set up in America. At present, senior officials of the Quebec hydro are chief organizers of the provincial Liberal party.

The empire of the Liberal party would then cover the bungling press as well as the state radio and T.V. to reach finally every Quebec home with an electric shock. Then, a man such as Rene Levesque would only have to become leader of the Liberal party and, inspired by his idol Senor Castro, he could invite him in and hold wide open the doors of the province of Quebec to communist infiltration.

Under the pretext of giving back to the French Canadians the control of natural resources which are rightly theirs, Quebec Liberals will in fact succeed only in stirring up against us all the interests which control over 80 per cent of our industries.

I wish to warn my fellow citizens against this group which is trying to make one section of our people rise against another, and particularly against some separatists or leftists who endeavour to set the Canadians of one group against those of another, and who have only one political purpose in mind, that of being the party in office at any cost.
I wish to denounce such an attitude and such people, and I shall keep on reminding the house that the best interests of all Canadians resides not in being divided but in being united. We have to find a solution to very serious problems, and it is not in trading upon the feelings of a minority that we shall manage to establish that unity we must reach in Canada if we are going to keep prosperity in our country-

The misconception that leads us to believe that we are the slaves of a superior race must disappear.
The Address-Mr. Bourbonnais
Our elite, our leaders will have to convince the French Canadians that success can be reached only through hard work and sustained efforts, rather than make them believe that the government is the only spring-board at their disposal to succeed, and also to remind them that they will have to be qualified enough so that the government will need them, and not the other way around. It is not by coveting another man's wealth that one gets rich, but in improving one's knowledge and working as hard as the other man.
Mr. Speaker, when the politicians, especially those in the Liberal party, stop lying to the people of Quebec and promising them the moon to get votes, when they stop laughing at the French Canadians and setting them against each other in order to come back to power at any price, in order to secure greater benefits from it at our expense, when they become more objective and stop fomenting hatred and, consequently, revenge, the French Canadians, instead of squabbling among themselves about matters of little importance, will stop taking opposite sides in matters of municipal or parochial importance, in sports, and even in business and industry. When the Liberals cease to divide French Canadians, we will stop wasting our time and we will direct our effort towards the improvement of our own business, without trying to blame anyone else for our failure.
What was granted to the Quebec French Canadians in the past five years of Conservative government compares most favourably with what was done over the 22 years of Liberal dictatorship in the Canadian parliament.

Mr. Speaker, listen to the hon. members opposite laughing; they remind me of braying donkeys.
As I say, I hold no brief for the Social Credit philosophy, but I will try to throw some light on a real phenomenon: the election of 26 Quebec Social Credit members to this house. Similar causes led me to enter politics. Being the scion of a Liberal family, raised in a Liberal atmosphere, I was so disgusted by the lies and demagogic doings of the Liberal leaders I knew that I chose to join the Conservative party whose doctrine, in my opinion, was the closest to the Liberal philosophy, but whose leaders showed much more dedication to the people and interests of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, when the Liberals were in office in Ottawa, and more particularly in Quebec, they never stopped exploiting the people's credulity and making the less prosperous people believe that the government could change their fate and settle them in the garden of Eden. During that time they encouraged the development of financial and industrial trusts, they nominated their friends to all the high positions in the federal government and in a great number of private

companies. To stay in office, they resorted to all conceivable means, the most efficient of which were demagogy and promises.
In 1958, the Canadian people rejected them as a whole. And when the member for Laurier refers to the Social Credit group as being isolated at the far corner of the house, it comes to my mind that during the last parliament, the Liberals were not only isolated but wedged in, as in a nut-cracker, between the N.D.P. and the Conservative block. In 1960, another storm of demagogy, abuses and promises swept over the province of Quebec. When the Liberal thunder stopped and the voters realized that they had been submitted to another brainwashing, in addition to a four year Liberal campaign on the radio, on television and in various newspapers, against the Conservatives and their leader, the right hon. Prime Minister, a great number of people in Quebec lost faith in the traditional parties and thought they had nothing to lose by voting Social Credit. If there are now 26 Social Credit members in the house, it is those Liberal gentlemen's doing, and if they go on in the same way there will be 60 after the next election.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that those surviving among the 75 drips mentioned in his paper Le Devoir, by Andre Laurendeau, when speaking of the 75 Liberal candidates in the province of Quebec during the last election, will benefit from that lesson and will not follow in the steps of their leader, the number one demagogue of Canadian politics, the Picasso of politics.
Instead of wasting their time in looking for a bogey and trying to belittle personalities, I would advise them to read a booklet dealing with Frank Buchman's comments on Moral Re-Armament: they certainly would learn some very profitable lessons in doing so.
Mr. Speaker, I said a moment ago that I had no intention of defending Social Credit. I must tell you that I do not share their views in the monetary field. Yet, those people have come here with a far greater sincerity than all our friends in the Liberal opposition. They came here to stand up for what they saw at home, to defend the small people who have been abandoned, flouted, and to whom the Liberals had been telling lies for much too long a time. Fleming before this house at the earliest opportunity a measure to approve the collection of taxes which have been imposed by order in council, as part of the austerity program, denies to this house the exclusive constitutional right to approve the imposition of additional taxation which is the foundation of our system of responsible government."

He seems to be directing his attack against two elements in the exchange program that the government introduced in June. These two elements are the import surcharges and the reduction made in the exemption on tourist purchases. I propose, Mr. Speaker, to deal with this subject in relation to the legal and constitutional questions that are raised.
In relation to these two elements in the government's program may I speak first of all of the legal aspects. My first point is that we have proceeded on the advice of the law officers of the crown in the proper manner, and the advice we have is that the measures which were introduced by orders in council in June, which took effect one minute after midnight on June 25, are proper and legal; that the government had full power to proceed to pass those orders in council, and that those powers so exercised were conferred upon the governor in council by parliament. There can be no question about the validity of those orders in council.
As to the import surcharges-

I proceed now, Mr. Speaker, to the other question that has been raised, what one might call a constitutional question, as to whether the governor in council has somehow or other imposed taxation here. It is an accepted rule, which no one questions, that taxation can only be imposed by act of parliament. That question was settled early in the seventeenth century. I remind hon. members that in 1628, and again in the bill of rights, the rule was then declared at Westminster, and has been observed since, or should have been, until the time when hon. members opposite were forming the government-and I shall have something to say about what happened in 1947-that no man should be compelled to make any gift, loan,


or pay tax without consent by act of parliament. Therefore there is no question about the principle.
Had parliament not chosen to confer on the governor in council the powers that were exercised in June there would certainly be no right to impose import surcharges or to reduce the exemptions accorded to returning tourists. Those measures depend for their validity upon these enactments of parliament. I have referred to these enactments, and the authority is clear. Therefore there is no constitutional issue raised here, none whatever.
Parliament does not always proceed to impose taxation in a direct manner. There are various examples one could point to in the enactments of parliament where the taxation is not directly imposed or the rate directly established. I take time to mention only several of these. Section 4 of the Customs Tariff authorizes the withdrawal by the governor in council of tariff benefits, resulting in increased tariffs. Section 7 of the Customs Tariff authorizes the governor in council to impose a surcharge in certain cases. The Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act, which was on the statute books of this country for many years, authorized the governor in council to make regulations imposing export duties on power exported from Canada, and this authority was continued by section 4 of the Exportation of Power and Fluids Importation Act which was passed in this parliament in 1955. Perhaps hon. members will remember that year when a tax was, in fact, imposed by the governor in council under the authority of that provision, and this tax was made statutory by section 8 of the Excise Tax Act amendments which I had the privilege to introduce in 1959. The Export Act authorizes the governor in council to declare an export duty chargeable upon logs and pulpwood exported from Canada, and also authorizes the governor in council to impose export duties on certain ores and metals.
Therefore let it not be forgotten that when parliament imposes taxation it does not in all cases do so in direct terms. These are examples where parliament has given power to the governor in council to proceed with the imposition of taxation and the variation of taxation. There is nothing extraordinary about the legislation which parliament passed, or about the powers which were conferred by these parliamentary enactments on the governor in council, and which were exercised in June last.

I shall have something to say about the question of confidence before I conclude my remarks. That is another matter.
Now, by way of emphasizing the course we have taken in 1962, I wish to compare it with the course that was followed by the Liberal government in 1947; because there have been some erroneous and misleading references during this debate to what happened in 1947.
Let us look at what happened in that year. First let me observe that there were three elements in the program introduced by orders in council of the government in 1947 to meet the foreign exchange emergency of that time. First, by order in council they reduced the tourist exemptions. Second, by order in council they prohibited the importation of certain goods; and third, they imposed special excise taxes on certain goods.
Those were the three elements in their program. As to the first of these elements, the reduction of the tourist exemptions, there was undoubtedly authority to do this under the Foreign Exchange Control Act of
1946,	which was still in force. I will have occasion to refer to that act further, and also to an undertaking that was given to the house when that legislation was under debate prior to its enactment.
As to the second element, the prohibition that was imposed by order in council on the import of certain goods, this was an order in council passed on November 12, 1947 which was not made public until November 17,
1947.	Under its powers prohibition was imposed upon the entry of certain goods into Canada.
The minister of finance of that day, both in his famous radio speech on the evening of November 17, 1947 and later in his speech in the House of Commons on December 16, 1947, said that the government had obtained legal opinion to the effect that the government had power under the statute I have

Mr. Speaker, we have made diligent search of the records in the Department of Justice, and we have not been able to find any such opinion. I can only conclude, then, that it was an opinion given orally to the minister of justice at that time by the law officers of the crown. But in this regard I do draw attention to a factor of very considerable importance in relation to the use by the government of the powers that they claimed to possess under the Foreign Exchange Control Act of 1946. When that measure, as I have said, was under debate in this house Mr. Ilsley, then minister of finance, gave the house this assurance. It is to be found at page 2547 of Hansard of 1946:
We have no intention of using this exchange control legislation to restrict anything but certain types of capital movements.
In passing the order in council the government of that day just tore to shreds and ribbons that solemn undertaking that it had given to parliament in 1946 when it asked parliament to pass the Foreign Exchange Control Act and confer very wide powers upon the governor in council. So whether there was a legal question or not, a very important question with regard to keeping good faith with parliament certainly was involved in that order in council which gave effect to the second element in the program of the government of that time, in relation to the prohibition of the import of certain goods.
The third element in that program, Mr. Speaker, was the imposition of special excise taxes as from midnight on that night of November 17, following the radio speech delivered by the minister of finance that evening. Those taxes then imposed were without a shred of legal justification; they were illegal.

speechtext:
When you have a chance to make a speech, we will listen to you. Rather than strive for independence, some people are willing to sacrifice their freedom for promised security, a form of security promised by government. What we need in Canada is a new sense of purpose, a genuine realization that we must work hard, and a realization that we can share only that which is first produced. We have been somewhat local in our thinking without realizing that the world is changing fast. New trading alliances among our friends threaten our traditional markets.
This fact was brought forcefully to my attention during the past few months, when I met with delegates from 17 commonwealth countries at a commonwealth parliamentary conference in London. We were there to discuss the future role of the commonwealth in the modern world. In my opinion, following this conference it was the intention of the United Kingdom to join the European common market as soon as convenient, if at all possible.
This attitude, of course, did not meet with the approval of any of the representatives of the other commonwealth countries. Our Prime Minister, when he recently attended the prime ministers' conference in London, took the same stand. I think it is his responsibility to make representations on behalf of Canadian industry, Canadian farmers, Canadian fishermen and Canadian labour. After all, this is one of the reasons prompting the United Kingdom to join the common market. She is attempting to gain greater economic benefits for her people. Would we expect our Prime Minister to do any less on behalf of Canadian citizens? However, a close study of the European common market indicates that this is a magnificent political achievement, and when you stand at the memorial at Verdun and realize that part of this transformation is the reconciliation of France and Germany, you then have a greater appreciation of the new spirit permeating Europe and of Britain's desire to become a part of this development.
Where does this leave us? We must be prepared, if Britain joins, for some loss of our privileged position in the United Kingdom

market, but Britain will continue to need many of the things we now export to her and trade may be less drastically affected than we might suppose. In fact, with Britain entering the common market it is possible her industries may increase their imports of raw materials from Canada. On the other hand, we must not underestimate our sales prospects in a western Europe enjoying rising prosperity and high living standards. However, our progress in this direction will depend upon the initiative of each and every one of us. We will havetogoafter these markets with well designed products at competitive prices and with vigorous and imaginative salesmanship. Obviously, the more successful we are in holding down our costs and improving our productivity, the more successful we will be in increasing our exports. This also implies progressive and forward thinking on the part of management plus a spirit of cooperation among labour.
This is the challenge faced by all Canadians, management and labour combined, if we are to successfully meet the threat to Canadian jobs posed by intensified foreign competition. This is a problem that not only concerns the government but is the concern of every Canadian; and when we realize we can only improve our living standards not by leaning on the government but by working harder and in greater harmony together, we will then achieve a new sense of national purpose. We must endeavour as a nation to conquer our unemployment problems, and this can only be achieved by providing improved opportunities in our primary and secondary industries.
The speech from the throne offers many incentives that will help bring this about, and it is indicative of the careful thought given to these problems by the Prime Minister and his cabinet. There is not sufficient time for me to comment on all the proposals in the throne speech, but I should like to deal with a few that are important to my province and to my constituency of Queens-Lunen-burg.
I note it is the intention of the government to take positive, constructive measures to strengthen Canada's balance of international payments. The recently stabilized exchange rate for the Canadian dollar has helped producers in all parts of Canada, both in the domestic and export markets, and is contributing as well to a large expansion in the Canadian tourist industry. This fact unfortunately became a political football in the recent election, with Liberal money being printed with caricatures of our Prime Minister and the then minister of finance on either side and showing a value of 92J cents. This Liberal money, Mr. Speaker, was of no more

value to Canadians than the Liberal promises were during the 22 years they were in office, though it was indicative of the childish attitude of the Liberal party toward the Conservative administration. I am certain this juvenile Liberal paper money did not gain any supporters in Queens-Lunenburg, for the voters in my constituency remember only too well the depreciation in the purchasing power of the Canadian dollar under 22 years of Liberal rule.
Inflation ran rampant under the Liberal government; it kept statisticians busy altering the cost of living index until we realized that in 1956 it took $1 to buy what 50 cents would buy 20 years before. However, the stabilized exchange rate has been beneficial to our great and expanding fishing industry, our pulp and paper industry and our tourist industry. It is the tourist industry that offers still greater potential income for Nova Scotians, and as the industry expands it strengthens Canada's balance of payments.
One project that would be helpful to our tourist industry is a second ferry between Nova Scotia and Massachusetts. I am fully aware that such a link has not always been successful in the past. Services once provided between Yarmouth and Boston declined and were withdrawn. However, I believe these connections were casualties of changing times, and that a second ferry service today between Nova Scotia and the United States would be beneficial to both countries. The present service between Yarmouth and Bar Harbor has not been able to accommodate the demands of traffic, especially in the summer months. It is primarily a service to Canada, for it favours drivers from Ontario and Quebec. I find no fault with this, but travellers from Massachusetts find it necessary to stay somewhere overnight in order to proceed to Nova Scotia, and they may as well drive all the way to the maritimes.
I believe a daylight run from Nova Scotia to Gloucester would be a great convenience. It would eliminate the need for costly sleeping accommodation on board the ferry, and it would open up for us the potential tourist market in the greater Gloucester, Boston and New York area, where over 50 million people reside. In addition, the ferry would provide quicker delivery for the products of our expanding fresh fish industry, which are daily gaining in favour and enjoying increasing sales in the United States market. This link is essential to provide an increased flow of trade between these historic trading areas, and I hope the government will give favourable consideration to this proposal.

This is true also in the Caledonia area of Queens county. In former years many people were engaged in mixed farming, but recently some farmers have become more selective and have specialized in the raising of hogs, cattle or poultry. I believe there is a greater awareness today of the fact that agriculture is no longer a method of earning supplementary income. Our Lunenburg and Queens county farmers are now looking at agriculture in its proper light, as an industry, a big industry, that can provide a way of life with peace of mind and material benefit unsurpassed by any other type of employment.
Gross farm income last year from all agricultural production in Nova Scotia exceeded $60 million. Nova Scotia has long been recognized as a grass country, a province in which grass grows probably as well as it does anywhere in the world. Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like to join those who preceded me in offering you my congratulations on being in the exalted position for which you have been chosen. To say this is more than a formality on my part, because I have a genuine respect for the extraordinary qualities required in the discharge of your duties. I am also pleased with the choice of Deputy Speaker, a man I have had occasion to admire as committee chairman during the last session of parliament. To him and the other presiding officers of the house I wish a successful tenure of office, be it short or long. The mover and seconder of the address in reply also deserve congratulations for having performed a very creditable job.
The speech from the throne has been described in various terms. One hon. member has described it as a speech to fit the times. Some call it a bold speech; others regard it as a very cautious one. We on this side of the house claim it was inadequate to meet the problems confronting the nation. However,
The Address-Mr. Badanai it did contain a few constructive suggestions such as enlargement of the industrial development bank and the provision of more funds for the Farm Credit Corporation. The establishment of an Indian claims commission and a national medical council are proposals which will not find any opposition from us, but the suggestion to call a dominion-provincial conference on the choice of a national flag does not commend itself. In view of our critical financial situation and other matters of vital importance, time should not be wasted in debating such a proposal, time which can be used to better advantage in finding ways and means to correct the many ills of the nation.
So far as I am concerned there is no time to waste on awakening old animosities and wrangling about the merits of designs for a distinctive flag. As a matter of fact I believe we already have a flag which is recognized everywhere throughout the world. I am referring to the old red ensign. Nations are moving towards the idea of a unified world in which the importance of national flags is diminishing.
The idea of dividing the Northwest Territories may be sound but I doubt the wisdom of prematurely preparing the territories for provincial status until they have sufficiently large populations to justify such a move. Otherwise additional governments could only mean additional burdens which the taxpayers of the country would have to meet.
We can all agree that the speech was long and replete with generalities and hints of measures which had a familiar ring, but it contained nothing of a definite nature outlining a program designed to inspire the Canadian people with a call for action, to which every adult Canadian could respond, in order to ensure a return of confidence in an economy badly shaken by the revelations made by the Prime Minister only a few days after the election last June.
The speech contained many items, some of which are of a rehashed nature and some new, intended to provide some vehicle that will bring back order out of the chaotic conditions for which the present government must accept responsibility. Gone are the days when it was convenient for the Prime Minister and his supporters to blame the former Liberal administration for everything that went wrong. It is surprising-indeed, it was surprising to me-that in the long list of intended legislation the question of immigration was completely ignored. Reform of the immigration laws of our country should be one of the items of consideration by this twenty fifth parliament, if it is allowed to proceed for any length of time.

The Address-Mr. Badanai
The present policy, based on the unemployment situation, is unrealistic. It perpetuates a state of fear, a lack of confidence, and general disintegration of the idea that the twentieth century belongs to Canada The high sounding words with which the new regulations were announced during the last parliament, such as "no more discrimination against prospective immigrants on grounds of race, colour, creed or country of origin" were soon discovered to be nothing more than a smoke screen to conceal the substitution of one form of discrimination for another.
Under the new regulations, which went into effect on February 1, 1962, an unsponsored person can qualify for entry into Canada on his own merit. But this is the real catch. Unless the applicant can qualify under the regulations, which spell out certain skills, and unless he or she is a doctor, nurse, medical laboratory technician, dietician, teacher, accountant, qualified social worker, priest, minister or a lawyer, he or she need not apply. As I look around this chamber-I do not have to look very far-1 fail to see a shortage in the legal profession.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think immigration should be restricted to people of particular trades or professions. We should be willing to admit to our shores people of enterprise and imagination who will continue to build Canada in the spirit of the early pioneers. At least, I thought that was what the Prime Minister wanted when he was in opposition. To suggest that only immigrants with certain skills need apply, under Canada's long term immigration policy, is to cripple the future growth of this country for generations to come. The present regulations can only succeed in keeping people out. The very idea, Mr. Speaker, of the grading of applicants for admission to Canada, as cattle are graded for the purpose of exhibition, will not encourage anyone to seek entry into our country.
Countless people in Canada-and I venture to say that some may be now sitting in this parliament-who have succeeded and have made good Canadian citizens might not have got into the country if they had been subjected to the test which this government has applied to all prospective immigrants.
The Prime Minister and most of his supporters were in favour of a generous immigration policy before they were elected to form a government. They had nothing but condemnation for the Liberal government for not allowing more people into the country. As far back as February 25, 1953, the Prime Minister said, as reported in the Globe and Mail, that complete disintegration of Canada's economic structure was predicted unless its population jumped to 40 million in the next 25


years. He said, "We cannot sit on the storehouse of the world with a population of 15 million without inviting disaster."
Mr. Speaker, at the rate we are admitting immigrants into this country, and allowing for a generous birth rate, it will be, not 25 years before we reach a population of 40 million, but even 50 years will not do it.
On April 27, 1957, the Toronto Telegram reports the Prime Minister saying that increased population was required if Canada's development was to keep pace with her vast resources; that a Conservative government would apply a vigorous immigration policy in co-operation with the provinces, and that the Immigration Act would be overhauled. "Canada must populate or perish."
Well, Mr. Speaker, a Conservative government has been in power for more than five years but no change of policy designed to encourage more immigrants has taken place. The actual policy which has been in operation for five years can hardly fit the statement the Prime Minister made when addressing a gathering in London, Ontario, on May 7, 1961. He then said:
Unless we populate and use the God-given resources of ours, we stand in peril of perishing under communism.
Mr. Speaker, because of high unemployment there has developed in some quarters doubt as to the advantages of immigration, this despite the fact that Canada's domestic market is more than a million consumers greater because of the former Liberal government's immigration policy in the decade between 1947 and 1957.
Those who question the benefits of immigration would do well to consider the opinion of the eminent British economist, Colin Clark. Professor Clark holds the view that population growth, far from being something to be feared, should be welcomed. His reasoning is that pressure of population has proved a beneficial force, stimulating nations into creating a more productive economy, improving their cultural patterns and in many cases moving toward the direction of a freer market. In other words, immigration pays off.
Every immigrant coming to Canada has a certain value and is an asset of merit. Our entire future is concerned with this. We must have immigration to prosper. The Immigration Act, which was to receive an overhaul, as I have already indicated, is still intact. What has been added to it is a set of restrictive measures based on the hypocritical statement that racial discrimination has been eliminated, when in fact the end result proves that the device was designed to keep people out. The government must bear responsibility

for the unenlightened performance of the department. It is to be hoped that under the direction of the new minister a more realistic attitude toward immigration will be adopted.
It is hard to believe, but figures speak for themselves and indicate that this government, while professing to be in favour, appears to be set against an increase or a growth in population. Every action taken so far during the past four years has given ample cause to suspect an unwarranted reluctance to formulate a policy which would allow more people into the country. No one can successfully deny that present regulations as administered at the discretion of the minister are such as can be turned on and off like a water hose in one's garden. There has never been a time when arguments could not be raised against immigration. Some hold the view that immigrants are, in effect, job takers and that the more immigrants allowed in the greater the threat to employment and living standards. Extensive studies made by responsible persons have shown the opposite to be true. One of these studies revealed that in 1961 some 50 per cent of a group of 6,969 immigrants applying for citizenship in Toronto and Montreal had become employers and were themselves providing work for no less than 3,070 people. Mr. Speaker, these facts deserve to be made more widely known if the misconceptions which are so prevalent are to be corrected.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring to the attention of the new Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Bell) an editorial which appeared in the Fort William daily Times Journal of August 4, 1962. It says:
During the 12 months ending June 1 of this year,
70.000	immigrants entered Canada. During the same twelve months 72,000 people emigrated from Canada to the United States and other countries. Roughly two thirds of our loss of 72,000 went to the United States. The situation calls for sober study by national administrators at Ottawa.
Since the close of the last war, those prospects brightened considerably. Year after year around
200.000	people arrived annually from overseas to join us in the development of the country.

The prevarications of the Social Credit members who sustained the government last week defeated the Liberals' no confidence motion. But they do not prove that Mr. Diefenbaker has the confidence of the country.

I have two and possibly three objectives to gain in the time that is available to me. First, I wish to make a comment or two on the debate thus far. We in this group have noticed that several of the Liberal members, particularly those from the province of Quebec, have spent nearly all of their time acting as though the Social Credit party now forms the government. It seems to us that they are indicating that some members in the party they represent have hurt them in recent days. I suggest that their attempts to move in this house one amendment after another indicate that they seem to be in a tremendous hurry to have this parliament dissolved and to be getting on with the business of another election. This attitude may change in the next few days after the culmination of an event that is now taking place in the province of Quebec and is occupying the attention of their colleagues there. There must be some reason for this rush to get back to the hustings.
Certainly we in this party have taken the attitude that we were elected as members of this parliament, as representatives of our constituencies, to carry on the business of

government to the best of our abilities. We recognize the fact that during this past summer we were not elected in sufficient numbers to form the government and therefore we do not assume responsibility for the policies followed by this government. At the same time charges have been made that we are betraying our mandate. I suggest that the greatest betrayal of our mandate would be to support the Liberals in advancing any of their policies in this parliament. The Liberal party did not receive a mandate to administer the affairs of the country. As has been mentioned on numerous occasions, this entire house is made up of minorities. If we were to accept their contention that the time is now ripe to seek dissolution and to go back to the country, I suggest that we would not be doing the responsible thing at this time. We in this party have assumed the responsible position of giving the government an opportunity to bring on their legislative program. At the same time we have reserved the right to examine that program. At some future time, if they do not attempt to correct some of the mistakes and mismanagement we have seen over the past four years, we would join with other opposition groups if they choose to bring on an election and to change the composition of this house. At the present time, however, there are 264 members elected in this house. If another election were called immediately, that is all we could elect. The people of Canada could elect only 265 members. We take the position that it is the responsibility of members who are now here to settle down, to give the government an opportunity, and to see what they have to offer. In addition to that, each one of the members of this group was elected primarily to give effect to the policies of the Social Credit party. Previously in this debate we moved an amendment designed to give effect to them. Our subamendment was lost. However, as I say, we were committed to advocating those policies and we did so.
I should now like to turn to one or two things that have been said respecting these policies we have been advocating. We would do this a little differently from what they have advocated. We have said that it is now and should be the responsibility of the Bank of Canada to set up a branch for the purpose of making long range capital available to the municipalities for the social structures that most municipalities need. We believe that if this were done long range social capital could be provided at a lower rate of interest and, further, that this kind of expansion at the municipal level, in the form of schools, hospitals, roads and all the responsibilities of municipal government, could be one of the greatest moves in alleviating the unemployment situation that could be taken in Canada today.
We are not advocating that the federal government should make this capital available on the basis of straight grants because we have had experience in this regard in the province of Alberta. We set up a municipal finance corporation in the last two or three years but previous to that large scale loans and grants were made directly through the department of municipal affairs, and the problem in making direct grants for these purposes is that there is not an equitable

The Address-Mr. Olson distribution of the funds. It boils down to a position of those municipalities that ask the most actually receiving the most.
We believe that the assets of the federal government through the Bank of Canada belong to all of the people and if in one given year or cycle one municipality or one area of Canada asks for more and it is considered prudent to give them more the money should be made available by way of an interest bearing loan so it will be recoverable. I have one other very important matter that I should like to bring before the house. I refer to the concept of agriculture and what has been received by agriculture from the government during the past four or five years. I want to quote one or two passages from Hansard to give some background to the point I wish to make. As found on page 75 of Hansard the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) had this to say:
I saw the Leader of the Opposition on election nipht, Mr. Speaker, when he believed he was going to be occupying this seat. That is before the western farmer came in.
It is perhaps the prerogative of the Prime Minister and other members of the Conservative party to take as much credit for their political activities as they wish. I believe though that there is a misconception in the minds of most Canadians not engaged in agriculture to the extent that they believe that agriculture has received a far larger share of the funds of the federal treasury than they are entitled to. I think the Conservative party should be deeply indebted to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) for getting so much mileage out of so little fuel; but that is not what concerns me. What concerns me at the moment is that in the future the position of the Minister of Agriculture is, I think, going to be jeopardized to some extent because of the widespread feeling that farmers are already getting too much. I quote now from an editorial headed "Let's Get This Straight" in the Western Producer of August 2, 1962:


We are completely fed up with some of the glib assumptions made by the people who. before, during and after the election campaign undertook to size up the prairie vote situation by implying the Conservatives "bought" the farmers' vote with large and unwarranted government "handouts".
Readers may remember some of the "funny" men on election night remarking that you couldn't get in the door of the average prairie farm house without kicking aside the pile of government cheques. Another wisecrack-at least we think this is what was intended-was to the effect that every time a farmer opened his mail box at the post office a few more "handout" cheques tumbled out-[DOT]
But as lately as last week-
The reference is to the last week of July.
-we read in an eastern newspaper a "learned" dissertation on how much government money it cost to buy the prairie farm vote.
I know that a great deal was said during the election campaign about the fact that the government of the day was passing out large amounts of money and that in fact they had established agricultural policies that were giving the farmers a larger share of the national income than at any time in history.
For example, on page 98 of Hansard I find the Prime Minister had this to say:
Prices have increased to such an extent that in every part of Canada farmers are receiving more for their production than they could have hoped for a matter of a few years ago.
In the next column on the same page, I find he says this:
I believe that everywhere across this country people are deeply indebted to the Minister of Agriculture for the effort he has made.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I looked at some of the statistics with respect to the actual cash income of farmers in Canada for the period that was under consideration during the election campaign. This is what I found. For example, from the sale of wheat during the first three months of this year, January to March 1962, farmers received $66,026,000 as opposed to $82,336 for the same period in 1961. In the matter of Canadian wheat board payments, during the period of January to March 1961, there was distributed to farmers $37,-
750,000	to the farmers, and in the corresponding period in 1962 this figure of $37,750,000 had been reduced to only $17,000. I want to say that there was $3,853,000 paid out in wheat board payments on oats in 1961. During the same period in 1962 there were no payments at all. The total cash income from the sale of farm products in Canada for that group under the heading of "Crops" for the period 1962 was $189,042,000 as opposed to $270 million for the same period in 1961.
I think it is abundantly clear, therefore, that the farmers have not received a disproportionately high share of the national income during this year, 1962.
I want to be fair in this to the Minister of Agriculture because it is my hope that in

setting this record straight I will be able to assist him in his avowed purpose, indeed in his obligation, to pursue policies beneficial to agricultural producers in all parts of Canada. I want to say, to be perfectly fair, that during the next quarter, from April 1 to June 1, the statistics which have been made available to us recently indicate a substantial increase in these Canadian wheat board payments. For well over a thousand years democracy has been well served by the parliamentary system, but of recent months, recent weeks and recent days I have come to worry a little bit about the future of this system. This chamber is not a circus. This is a place where I trust


able men, dedicated men, come to present a program for maintaining democracy in an able, conscientious and decorous way.
Democracy is not perfect; it never will be. We as members are not perfect and never will be; but surely we can try to maintain the high standards which our ancestors and our fathers, and which many present members of the house have maintained up to this time. I beg of hon. members to keep this in front of them. There is something going on here more than the mere arguing about the price of hogs and interest rates, or the advancement of new ideas on the way in which we run the country. Our very freedom depends on the way we run this house, and unless we maintain the confidence of the people of Canada it is better that we should stay at home.
I carried on a positive campaign in order to be re-elected to this house. I believe it is somewhat of a surprise to some that I still sit here, but I think the reason I was reelected is that what I preach I practise. I do not criticize for criticism's sake; but now I am going to go round this chamber a little and do what I rarely do, and that is criticize the critics.
The hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) said the other night, at page 227 of Hansard for October 4, as it is reported- and these were not her exact words as I heard them, but I take them as they were recorded-
All members of the opposition were elected for one purpose, and that was in opposition to the government.
I say to the electorate, to the people of Canada and to every hon. member in the house that this is a very negative approach to politics. I suggest there is a need for an opposition. We need at least two parties so that we can file down the legislation which we present, or which we intend to present, and make it work for the good of the whole country. No such policy of pure opposition can do that.
I believe there are hon. members opposite who have a contribution to make. I think there are hon. members in all four parties who have a contribution to make. I want them to have an opportunity to make it and when they make that contribution I will vote for it. I am no narrow party man. I was not born a Tory. I was born a Canadian and it is from reading the history of our country and this party that I still stand on this side of the house and give my allegiance to our great leader and the party he leads. When this party fails to-run the country the way it should, I will cross the floor of the house and I will sit

alone because at the present time I see no alternative to the leadership or to the policies of this party which I support.

They are going to criticize our monetary policy. They think we can live like an island in the western world with new, phony monetary policies. We know we cannot. Our monetary policies are not perfect; our capitalistic system is not perfect. But it has produced the finest opportunity for ordinary, working Canadian boys or girls to develop their own personality and to make their own way in the world. I see no alternative to this.
I am surprised to see a great party, such as was the Liberal party when led by Gladstone in England and Laurier in Canada, descend to any kind of a working agreement with avowed socialists. I am, most seriously surprised, ladies and gentlemen, because-

I am, most seriously surprised, Mr. Speaker, because it does not offer me free choice with my time and talents. If hon. members do not think that socialism is nothing but a white horse of Troy and inside are red soldiers, read your history. Read the past and present history of socialism and then ask these people in the corner what they intend to do from here on in.
I wish their leader were here to answer this question. I wish he were here to tell me whether he adheres to the same old avowed stand of the socialists in Canada. I refer hon. members back to that great spiritual leader of theirs, Mr. Woodsworth-and this has never been refuted or denied-when he was asked whether force would be necessary. He said, "I hope not, but it may well be necessary". If any hon. members in the corner of the chamber want the quotation, I have it here and I can give them the date, time and place. It was in this house. However, I have not the time to give it now; I have some things to say which are even more positive than the things I have said already. But those words are there.
Therefore I say that we want something besides mere criticism from those hon. members or I will never cross the floor of the house to sit with them; that is quite certain. I do not have to. But I promise those hon. members that I will, if they can come up with a better program, better leadership and better service to the Canadian people. If they can do that, I will join them, when I have lost confidence in this government-which I have 27507-3-21i
The Address-Mr. Bigg not. Then I will sit alone in this house, and I believe that as long as I take this stand, as long as I am at least one of those people who came here to do a positive job, I will be here until I am ready to retire.
Have we a positive program? We have. What is this positive program? It is a go-ahead program along the same lines as we have had in the last five years. I speak principally of agriculture because this is a matter about which I know something. I suggest hon. members in this house would do better if they talked about matters they knew something about. If you do not know anything about farming, keep quiet about it. I know that is why some hon. members opposite have kept quiet in recent days, because they have no agricultural policy and they have never had one satisfactory to the people of Canada. They are strangely silent about this fact. But the farmers of Canada know they have never had the attention paid to their problems that they have received from this government. We have given that attention to their problems. It is suggested that we have overdone it, but I do not think we have.
There are many small farmers, family farmers in Canada today who have new hope. They have not a cinch. You still have to work on the farm; you still have to milk the cows, raise the pigs and bring in the crops-and they know it. We are not offering these people something for nothing, and they know it. We are offering them hope for some kind of square deal. Western Canada is getting on its feet-I can assure hon. members that it is-and we are proud of that record. If eastern farmers are not as much ahead as they should be, I for one will do all I can to give them the same deal as the western farmers, and a better deal if it is needed. I do not think we have done everything for the farmers of Canada that could be done, but we are going to do as much as we can.
I can go through my campaign speech. It consisted of one sheet of paper. That was because I come from a farming district where agriculture is the lifeblood of the people. I campaigned from one sheet, the promises of our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker)-that no longer would the farmers of Canada be the orphans of this country; that we would try to give them a fair share of the national income.
You can take figures and juggle them; you can make them prove anything you like. I am not going to talk about figures; I am going to talk about human values. The small farmer of western Canada today is not ashamed to hand his farm over to his son. Four years ago you could have bought land from one end of

The Address-Mr. Bigg this country to the other; they were glad to let you take it. Today, try and get them off the farm.
The answer is there. Their sons are coming home from the oil fields, the bonanzas and the gold creeks and want to stay home with dad. They want to take advantage of our agricultural policies. Today a young man in western Canada can stay on the farm and make a living. We are going to see that we do all we can to make that living even better. We are proud of selling their wheat; we are proud of giving them stabilized prices, and we are going to do more and more to improve world markets.
I am not afraid to criticize this government at any time. As I have said, if they do not do the things I want them to do, I let them know it. They will tell you that. I have been in the Prime Minister's office and have spoken to him about things of which I did not approve. Yes, little, human errors, creep in. What kind of a reception did I get? Was I pushed out? No, I was listened to. On one or two occasions I think I had something to offer, and my suggestions were acted upon.
I am not going to bore hon. members with repeating them today, but the people of western Canada know; the small farmer in my district knows, and he is going to keep on sending me back here just as long as I give him this kind of service. These people are not going to turn me out for any member of any one of the other three parties until they can come up with something different. They are not going to get me out by slurring my personal character, and attempts were made to do this. They are not going to get me out by slurring the Prime Minister's character, and those attempts were made. They are not going to get me out by slurring the Conservative party, because the people of Canada know we are the only party offering a positive program for agriculture. They may be disappointed that we did not give them perfection or a bonanza. There is no such thing. There is no short cut to a higher standard of living and security. It takes hard work. You cannot do it by turning a crank; you cannot do it by taxing the rich. We can only do it by each and every one of us getting back to good, hard work.
We have an unemployment problem and there is a great onus upon this government, as there is on all governments, to find employment for every man and woman in Canada who wants to work. I suggest that today we have been lax. We have been too paternal. We have legislated people into idleness. One of our main jobs-and here I am throwing the ball right to our own quarterback and

his team in front of us-is to do something to avoid legislating people into idleness.
Let us take the Unemployment Insurance Act and look at it again. Let us make it an insurance act, and not a welfare fund. Where welfare is needed, let us have it; but let us not legislate people into idleness. How are we going to do it? I can suggest one or two improvements. Let us make it an incentive to stay at work. Let us make a man's contribution less if he is not always dipping into the fund. Let us make it tough to draw on the fund for those who are just milking the people of Canada and lying down on the job. We are going to tackle that problem. We are going to do what we can.
The next thing is, what can business do to employ more people? They can become more efficient. They can show leadership in this matter. Again I throw the ball to the government and say, give incentives to small business, to medium business and even to big business to encourage better production in Canada.
How are we going to do this? I am not an expert on taxes. I know that we have to raise taxes and raise incentives. But I suggest that the tax structure of the country could be tailored to encourage Canadian investment in Canadian companies, and to encourage our own businesses to improve production and put more Canadians to work. I think this should be encouraged by tax concessions. I suggest that if this is done and if the tax concessions which we give lead to investment in our own factories, and in turn provide jobs, it will all come back on the payrolls.
I will have to hand this to the opposition. I do not usually give them many compliments, but after the war they did send the veterans back to school; and I am sure that if you were to look at the records of those veterans, they paid back in income tax over and over again the very cost of this schooling. I suggest that we take a page out of their book and give tax concessions and tax incentives to the young businesses of Canada, the growing baby industries, and give them a chance to get on their feet. In this way, when they are employing more Canadians and making more money, the country will get it back, and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Flemming) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) will see that it has been a good investment.
Hon. members ask us to take bold steps. Well, they are the members of this house. When we take bold steps, they must have the courage to be Canadians first and Liberals, Social Crediters or N.D.P.'s second, and vote for these bold steps. I promise them today that I will do this thing. When my leader and his cabinet are bold, I am right in there for

them. I know sometimes these bold steps are gambles. If you build railroads into the north, if you build a trans-Canada highway through the northern part of the country, and take a chance that Canada will really be as wide as she is long, this takes foresight and vision, and it is partly a gamble. It cannot be done by a minority government alone; it would require statesmanship from everyone in this house. I pledge myself to do this. I promise hon. members that I will do it, and I expect them to do it. I am not cynical in politics.
I know that the great Liberal party has been a great Liberal party in the past, and I want it to be a great Liberal party in the future. To the Social Crediters I say this. If they are really Conservatives, as they say they are on the hustings, then join our party and be Conservatives. I ask them to forget the "funny money" policies which they know cannot work in the present structure of our country's economy. But they sit in the corner in smug complacency and know that they can criticize without fear, that they can never form a government but will sit here as long as they like and take advantage of the Conservative leadership in our country. If they are Conservatives let them be Conservatives, cut out the "funny money" policies and stand with us, if we ask them to, on principle.
It is a strange thing for me to sit in this house and listen to members of the "junker class" voting socialist. For what? Nobody can believe but that it is for pure political advantage of the day. I suggest that political advantage of the day will not last long, and the eggs you hatch may pick your carcass. Think that one over. They are strange bedfellows, the industrial leaders of our country and the gentlemen on my right, the socialists.
It is also strange to hear the policies put forward by our party criticized by those who have no such policies of their own. It is strange to hear about fears being spread across the world about our loyalty to the British crown. By whom? By those who in 1938 refused to allow empire airfields; by those who allowed only the volunteers of Canada to risk their lives and shed their blood. I was one of them. Do not talk about solidarity of the empire unless you are willing to stand alongside the flag under which I served; and until we get another one, one which is recognized in solemn parliament assembled, the red ensign is good enough for me. We buried my pals in it in the last war. We buried my uncles and my friends of another generation in another war. It is an honoured flag, and though we may not agree with the design of a new flag, the design is not all for which the flag stands. The flag is a symbol of our purpose in sacrifice and loyalty. It is red bunting which has been nobly served, and
The Address-Hon. P. Martin the sacrifices have been great. Until this parliament decides that that flag should be changed, I will be ready again to stand alongside it and give it anything which is needed.
How about others? Let us have no hypocrisy. Let us have no maudlin sentiments spelled out for political reasons. I will go further and say that whatever the flag is, let it be quartered with the fleur-de-lis, the sheaves of Saskatchewan, the fish of the mari-times or the timber of British Columbia. I do not say that I do not care what that flag is, but I do say that if this parliament, or the next parliament, or any parliament of Canada, ratifies that flag as a symbol of unity and service, I will be there to serve it whenever I am needed. And I will writhe in my seat when I think that anybody is using our flag as a spade or a club of disunity.
People out west where I come from know this. They know that I will never use it as a dividing line.
The promises that we have made in the past we have kept. The promises we make now in the throne speech hon. members can be assured will be kept. We cannot offer an easy way out, but we can offer hard work and a square deal.
