speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all may I be allowed to offer you my warmest congratulations on your appointment as Speaker of this house. I know that you will be the guardian of the rights and of the prerogatives of each and everyone of us in this house and that you will watch over the dignity of our debates.
Impartiality, patience and good will are the qualities required of a good Speaker. I am sure that you will show, to a high degree, those qualities by which your predecessors have deserved the commendation and the admiration of all.
(Text):
I should also like to congratulate the chairman of committees on his nomination, and to offer my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the speech from the throne for the very creditable way in which they performed their tasks.
And now, Mr. Speaker, I hope that no one who follows me, particularly from the far corner of the house, will complain if in what I have to say today I do not preface my observations by agreeing with them that we are faced as a country in our contemporary world with some very serious problems involving peace or war. But under our rules we are limited to 30 minutes at this particular juncture in our proceedings. Accordingly we have to allocate our time in order to observe the rule of relevancy and deal with matters im-

The Address-Hon. P. Martin mediately before us. But I take it there will be an opportunity, and I hope it will be soon, when we can discuss important aspects of the government's foreign policy and when we can take up some of the observations made, notably by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green). At the moment, however, we are dealing with an amendment moved by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacEachen) on Friday last in a memorable speech. I should like to recall to the house the wording of that amendment. It strikes at the very fundamentals of parliament, an institution which the hon. member who preceded me said now stood in jeopardy in this country. The terms of the amendment read as follows:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that the failure of Your Excellency's advisers to place before this house at the earliest opportunity a measure to approve the collection of taxes which have been imposed by order in council, as part of the austerity program, denies to this house the exclusive constitutional right to approve the imposition of additional taxation which is the foundation of our system of responsible government.
That is an amendment of the greatest importance. It is one that must be observed in its implications if we are to support the view that parliament indeed is an important institution in our national life, and that we must take every step to see that its strength and its integrity are protected. In this amendment the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond has done that. To any hon. member of this house who is disposed to vote against this amendment I suggest that a vote against the amendment will be a vote in favour of the government's austerity program which was brought about, not by a decision of this parliament but by process of an order in council.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming), who is the former minister of finance, this morning asserted that the government's austerity program had a legal basis. He did not offer any proof for that statement. He simply said that he had consulted with the law officers of the crown and that the three aspects of the government's austerity program met the requirements of the law as interpreted by the law officers of the crown. I wish to submit first of all to you, Mr. Speaker and to the house, that there is a contrary view.
What I wish to say today will be divided under two headings. First of all I question the legality of the government's austerity program under the two acts mentioned by the Minister of Justice this morning. Not only do I question the legality of a policy based on those acts but I say that, whether they were legal or not, under our constitutional practice there was an obligation on the government to come here at the earliest possible moment and


obtain from this parliament either rejection of the policy on which it had embarked or ratification of it.
First, as to the legality, may I say this. There can be no doubt that the argument by assertion made this morning by the Minister of Justice with regard to the incidents of 1947 does not in any way bolster the case which he sought to make. I say that section 4(1) of the Customs Tariff and section 22 of the Financial Administration Act do not contain authority from parliament to the governor in council enabling the governor in council to make the two orders which make up the surcharge on imports order. The Minister of Justice did not even allow for the possibility of difference of opinion in this regard. In that modest, humane way of his he simply said, "There is no doubt about the legality of what the government has done, take it from me". The minister of finance of another day, the present Minister of Justice, said, "Accept my word that there is no doubt about the legal basis of the action the government has taken".
Hon. members should recall that while parliament has delegated to the governor in council authority to reduce or to eliminate taxes under prescribed conditions, parliament has, by and large, retained unto itself the power to impose taxes. It must also be borne in mind that the Minister of Finance has the responsibility to parliament in the matter of raising or lowering the incidence of taxation; and the means by which this is done, Mr. Speaker, as you so well know, is a budget.
The Customs Tariff, I argue, is in no way concerned with Canada's balance of payments, notwithstanding the fact that it may contribute to what that balance may be. In section 4(1) of the Customs Tariff, parliament has delegated to the governor in council certain powers necessary to promoting Canada's trade with other countries. Raising duties against all countries will not in any way promote trade. Moreover, the language of section 4(1), as I see it, makes clear that the country to which preferred rates are extended or from which preferred rates are withdrawn must, under that section, be specifically named. The words employed are "extend to any"-which means any one-"country" and "withdraw from any country or all countries". Also, the benefits are spoken of as having been extended to or withdrawn from, "such country", not "such country or countries". I therefore say that the exercise of the authority conferred by section 4(1) requires the naming of a country or countries. Hence if no country is named, that section 4(1) does not give the sanction of parliament for the action taken.

I ask the Minister of Justice to produce, as indeed his leader asked the minister of finance of the day in 1947, the opinion of the law officers of the crown which states that section 4(1) gives this government the authority to impose surcharges as it did when parliament was not in session and when indeed as the government of this country it occupied an extremely tenuous position with only a minority support in this house.
With regard to section 22 of the other act, namely the Financial Administration Act, on which the minister and the government base their case, may I observe that the statute was enacted by parliament in order to give authority to the governor in council to deal with a comparatively few special cases involving a comparatively few individual importers and a comparatively small range of imported goods for a comparatively few special purposes, as stated in the act. If parliament had intended to delegate broad powers of extensive application to customs duties on imported goods, it would have done so in the Customs Tariff and the Customs Act. However, that was not done.
So I say that section 22 of the Financial Administration Act, on which the government relies as one of the two supporting measures, was not intended by parliament to delegate to the governor in council authority over a large portion of the customs tariff involving a large range of goods and all importers of those goods in a single case, which is not essentially one of the customs tariff itself but is a case of balance of payments. This, in a general statement, is my answer to the alleged legality of the measures on which the government relies for the course it has taken in a matter so seriously affecting the economy of our country, because of the austerity program which it has seen fit to adopt to meet the emergency created by our balance of payments position.
Having said that the course taken by the government is illegal, I now address myself to the other ground in the amendment before us, namely, that parliament should have been called together at the earliest possible moment so that the government could have laid before the house its proposals for taxation, its proposals by way of an austerity program to meet the serious situation that arose out of our balance of payments position. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fleming) says, compare what we did with what the minister of finance did in 1947. I do not want to base my case only on what was done, then, but I do now, because the Minister of Justice has invited it, want to compare in one very important respect the difference between what his government and he did and what Mr. Abbott did in 1947.
The Address-Hon. P. Martin
I have before me Hansard for December 16, 1947, page 359, and I wish to refer to an interjection by the then minister of finance explaining to the then hon. member for Calgary West what course the government was taking with regard to imposing taxes on the Canadian people. To hear the Minister of Justice one would think that what the Canadian government had done was to impose on the Canadian people taxation by radio and then to have come into the house later and have sought confirmation of that course. That is not what was done at all. There were three aspects in the emergency program of 1947. There was first of all the prohibition of imported goods from the United States. That did not involve any imposition of taxes. Second, there was the imposition of excise taxes and restrictions on the amount of money that tourists were allowed to expend in the United States when out of the country. The then minister of finance did not impose excise taxes by radio. Those taxes were imposed as part of the emergency program of that day as the result of a recommendation made by the minister of finance in this house. That is the difference. The minister of finance said at that time:
I say I am not claiming the right to tax the Canadian people.
The Prime Minister cannot take that position today because he has taxed the Canadian people, and taxed them without first of all obtaining approval or receiving from this house the necessary parliamentary sanction. Mr. Abbott went on to say:
It is nothing more than a notice that that tax will be imposed if parliament approves, and if parliament refuses to impose it nobody is under legal obligation to pay the tax today until parliament does approve. But I have notified the Canadian people, as is done when the budget resolutions are tabled, that I shall ask parliament to make this tax retroactive to the 17th day of November, when I gave the notice.
So I say to the Minister of Justice, there is no analogy in the two positions at all. If I had time I would remind the Prime Minister of what he said in that debate. I think perhaps what he did say is so relevant to the present situation that I should remind him of some things that he told the government of that day and which now have special relevancy to the very act about which we complain in this amendment. The Prime Minister said, as found on page 408 of Hansard for December 17, 1947:
Did the law officers of the crown in any way advise that it was possible for a minister of the crown, two or three weeks before the opening of parliament, to impose taxation from that date? I say to my hon. friends in the government of this country, that by that action they committed a crime against constitutional government in this

The Address-Hon. P. Martin country. And they wish us to act as rubberstamps and be accessories after the fact, by our vote now given, for conduct illegal to begin with.
Of course, as I have just indicated, his argument was faulty, but the recommendations that he made to the ministry apply to him today. We are not even rubberstamps. We are not given the opportunity of even passing on the illegal course which this government pursued in an unconstitutional way before parliament was called together on the 27th of September last. I will say for the record that no one has as commendable a record clearly establishing his love of parliament and all its institutions as the present Prime Minister, but I say to him with the greatest respect that since he became Prime Minister no one has initiated measures that are more inconsistent with this affection and this love of parliament than the right hon. gentleman himself. That is so at every turn. Here is what Mr. Abbott said as found on page 331 of Hansard for December 16, 1947:
I consulted the law officers of the crown, the deputy minister of justice, and I was advised that under the Foreign Exchange Control Act the governor in council had power to designate the currencies which could be used for imports and that that act was available for the purpose of imposing such restrictions. As I said a moment ago, it was never believed that the act contained those powers, and certainly the foreign exchange control board never had those powers and never wanted to have them.
But when it came to the matter of taxes, and hon. members will want to look at the exact provisions as contained in Hansard, they will find that on December 19, 1947, as found on page 535 of Hansard, Mr. Abbott moved certain amendments to the Excise Tax Act. These were debated by parliament. Many hon. gentlemen opposed those taxes. Parliament, however, approved of the government's policy and the imposition was made retroactive to November 17. Is the record not clear then that the government did no more than announce taxes outside of this house? There was an emergency. There was no other course open to the government at that time than the action taken by the then minister of finance. But at the earliest possible moment he came into this house and asked parliament to observe its traditional practice of giving its sanction to a proposal that would involve further taxes on the Canadian people.
That is the point. That is the point at issue in this amendment. That is the reason for the particular provision in the bill of rights to which the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacEachen) called our attention on Friday last. That is implicit in the bill of rights passed in this house at the instance of the right hon. gentleman two years ago and now so flagrantly being flouted


and violated by him in this particular instance. We say that parliament is a valuable institution. I certainly believe it is. I have spent more than 27 years in this house and I believe in this institution. But I know of no incident in the history of our country where parliament's rights have been more seriously violated-

-than in this particular form of taxation involving over $200 million by way of additional taxes imposed as the result of executive action without first of all having received the prior approval of parliament. This is bad in itself; this is wrong in every way. But in spite of this amendment, in spite of the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and others who have complained about the failure of the government to take parliament into its confidence at the earliest possible moment, even now we are not given any assurance by members sitting in the ministry that before this session has terminated they will have placed before us their program of taxation. Surely, we are not going to be denied this.
There are five ministers sitting in this house now. The leader of the house has just entered. They can tell us now whether or not parliament is going to be given the opportunity of passing on this particular program of taxes imposed on the Canadian people as part of the government's austerity program. I say to hon. gentlemen sitting at the extreme left on this side of the house, that they have been properly critical of the government's austerity program. They have said, through one of their leaders, that they will not stand for a program of austerity; that they believe such a program of a non-expansionist character is not in the interest of the economic welfare of Canadians at this time. I repeat that by voting against this amendment they are voting for this program of austerity. They are also denying to themselves and to other hon. members, the opportunity of passing judgment on the merits of these proposals.
It is not only that the government has acted illegally, it is not only that the government has not taken parliament into its confidence on a matter of vital concern to this house, it is something that goes even deeper than that, something that is involved in the historic conflict, over the centuries, between the crown and parliament. I refer to the right that was finally established, that of the House of Commons to assert authority over the government of the day in the matter of imposing taxes on the people who are subject to the direction and to the laws of parliament. This is what

is involved. Are we going to take the position that, notwithstanding the violation of this principle, something for which our ancestors have fought, we are not going to allow ourselves to be inconvenienced because of what might eventuate if we were to condemn the government by supporting this particular amendment? Of course it would be inconvenient. Of course the nation would have a period of suspense. I think particularly of the fathers of families, fathers over 50 who are told that they are too old to work. I think of youngsters getting out of school and having the keen edge of their enthusiasm for life dulled by finding themselves unwanted and unused in the labour market.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that primarily unemployment is a moral problem. Have we the imagination to realize the wastefulness and the wickedness of the enforced idleness of our fellow citizens? If we do realize this, have we the will to organize society so that our human resources shall be fully employed and unemployment in fact brought to an end? The reason that I am proud to be a member of this party is that I believe this party has recognized and accepted the only means that can end unemployment, the means of economic planning and expansion of the public sector of the economy to the extent required to give everyone willing and able to work a job.
I think also of those in my constituency who are crushed and defeated by the burden of debt and anxiety caused by expensive operations and medical bills. However, Mr. Speaker, it is my task today to call attention to what we believe are some

serious gaps in the program presented in the speech from the throne on other than economic matters. The speech from the throne refers to the proposed repatriation of the Canadian constitution. With this proposal we warmly agree. With the hundredth birthday of this country a few years away, it is indeed a strange anomaly that the control over the constitution of Canada rests, in form at least, with the imperial parliament of Great Britain long after Canada's full sovereignty was recognized by the Statute of Westminster.
But it is not enough to say that the Canadian constitution should be repatriated. The outlines at least of the proposed method of repatriation must be given. The constitution sets out the basis of our Canadian confederation and the relationship between the people of this country and their governments. It is of the utmost importance, therefore, that the constitution should entrench beyond the possibility of change the basic rights with respect to language, religion and education and should recognize fully the two nations and the two cultures that are the main streams of our existence. It is also our view that the amended constitution, to be made in Canada and by Canadians, should embody a genuine and constitutional bill of rights setting out the fundamental freedoms inherent in our parliamentary system. These freedoms, as members of the house know, are freedom of religion, freedom of speech and freedom of association. The present bill of rights, and I call the attention of the government members to this, is merely a declaratory statute capable of being overruled by this or subsequent parliaments and totally inoperative so far as provincial legislatures are concerned. If these fundamental rights and freedoms are contained in the solemn compact of our constitution, neither subsequent acts of parliament or the legislatures nor any subordinate authorities can invade them, and the courts will be able to act as the effective safeguard of our liberties to a degree that they cannot now.

The government was more anxious to allow passions to cool after the election, as the Prime Minister put it; or, as I would prefer to put it, the government was anxious to cling to power by taking steps to secure the support of a particular minority group. I call on all members of this house, Mr. Speaker, who believe that it is important to maintain the supremacy of parliament to vote for the amendment. I suppose it is too much to hope that the members of the government party will pay much attention to my suggestion, but I do most seriously suggest to the members of the Social Credit group that their vote on this amendment will be a test of the genuineness of their concern for parliamentary institutions, a test, moreover, of their faithfulness to their duties as a loyal opposition in this house.
May I make one last reference to the repatriation of the constitution? Much as we believe such repatriation to be desirable, it must not be done in such a way as to fasten a rigid and practically unamendable constitutional structure on this country or to give the power of veto to any one province in matters other than basic minority rights. In the proposals put before the in camera conferences of the attorneys general called by this government, such rigidity and such a veto were included.
The absurdity of such a veto power over any change whatever in constitutional provisions is made evident by a suggestion in the speech from the throne itself. The speech from the throne indicates an intention to put before parliament a resolution seeking an amendment to the British North America Act enabling parliament to legislate for contributory pensions. We in this group welcome this proposal. Supposing, however, all the provinces agreed to this change except one- and taking as an example the province of Newfoundland-would it be reasonable that one province, representing perhaps a small fraction of the people of Canada, could frustrate the will of the people of Canada as a whole in a matter in no way affecting basic provincial rights? Would it be reasonable to confer on the government of Prince Edward Island the right to veto the transfer to federal control of labour relations in nationwide industries such as steel and meat packing, which many believe can only be effectively handled at the national level?
The proposal for repatriation is a good one, but its method should provide for proper flexibility when required. There must also


be a full opportunity for public discussion and scrutiny of anything so vital to the good government of this country as the form of a fully Canadian constitution.
There was one other aspect of the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, that we in this group found gravely disappointing. I refer to the references to international affairs. The complacency of this government about international affairs and this country's role is, in our view, totally unwarranted. In the rapidly changing world of today, we have become an interdependent part of one world. All the people of the world are united by a common fear of nearly universal destruction. From day to day, the B-52's of the strategic air command fly an airborne alert over the United States and Canada, carrying, on the average, 25 megatons or 25 million tons of explosive power, more than 12 times the amount of explosive dropped by all the bombers in world war II, including the two atomic weapons.
The stockpile of nuclear weapons in the United States is, we are told by responsible authorities, equal to ten tons of explosive for everyone in the world, and the U.S.S.R. presumably does not lag far behind. We live in an explosive world. We in this group respect, as all Canadians do, the persistent efforts of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) to get the major nations of the world at least started on the road to disarmament. But there is no room for complacency. A striking gap in the speech from the throne is the complete omission of any reference to Canada's own part in the acquisition of nuclear weapons. Is the government still in the mist of indecision or has it made up its collective mind but is unwilling to tell the people of Canada of its decision?
We in this group believe that any addition to the security of the western alliance that Canada could bring by becoming, even to a limited extent, one of the nuclear club is far outweighed by the disastrous consequences involved in the further spread of the control of nuclear weapons to other nations. We regret that Canada did not take up clearly and unequivocally the Swedish initiative in the United Nations for the formation of a club, as it were, of non-nuclear nations pledging themselves to refrain from manufacturing or acquiring nuclear weapons and to refuse to receive them in their territory. The present degree of stability in the balance of deterrence may afford the human race a breathing spell when nuclear power to a significant degree is confined to two nations. The spread of nuclear weapons will quickly undermine any such stability of deterrence and make a nuclear holocaust set off by accident more probable than now. In any

event, what the western alliance lacks is not so much tactical or strategic nuclear weapons. What it lacks are highly mobile conventional forces. Canada's contribution to her own security and that of her allies will be far more significant if it takes the form of strengthening conventional forces for nonnuclear purposes.
We have to build, while we can, a world community so that we can eventually establish a rule of law over the nations. This is the task of this generation and it will tax our efforts and our imagination. Can Canada claim she is doing all that she can to create this world community? In an appeal issued by the World Council of Churches at New Delhi to all governments and people of the world, the following statement appears:
There is a great opportunity for constructive action in the struggle for world development. To share the benefits of civilization with the whole of humanity is a noble, attainable objective. To press the war against poverty, disease, exploitation and ignorance calls for greater sacrifice and for a far greater commitment of scientific, educational and material resources than hitherto. In this common task let the peoples find a positive program for peace, a moral equivalent for war.
In the Globe and Mail of May 31 of this year a reference appears to the testimony before a United States congressional committee by the United States aid chief, Mr. Frank Coffin. He said that Canada is far behind the leaders in the field of providing aid to underdeveloped nations. Canada, according to Mr. Coffin, gave .21 per cent of its gross national product, compared with .6 per cent by Britain and the United States, and .56 per cent by West Germany.
The New Democratic party at its founding convention said a reasonable standard for the amount of grants and long term interest free loans for economic aid was an expenditure equal to 2 per cent of the national income. We are convinced that with an expanding economy and full employment such a contribution is possible. Furthermore Canada might make a decisive contribution to the economic breakthrough of countries like India.
We live in days of challenge and we must make a creative response to it. That creative response will involve changing some of our traditional thinking and practices. Petty partisan bickering in this house, which unfortunately characterized the contributions to this debate by the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister, are not good enough in the world in which we live today.
I shall conclude my remarks by quoting some words of Barbara Ward, or Lady Jackson as she is also known, whose works have already been quoted in this debate. She uses these words:
The Address-Mr. Nowlan
The western citizen of today, if he is to face the world's crisis of freedom, cannot ignore the deepest ideals of his own free tradition. He must wish to recreate the face of the earth. He must see the human race as one brotherhood. He must set his abundance to work to end other people's misery and want. In this spirit freedom will conquer. Without it freedom hardly deserves the name.
I commend those words to this house.

Mr. Speaker, when rising to take part in this debate I of course want to pay the conventional, indeed more than the conventional tribute to the mover and seconder of the address on this occasion. I also, sir, want to pay my tribute to you for having achieved the position which you are occupying right now as Deputy Speaker of the House of Commons, and to the Speaker of the house who, for three or four years, was associated with me as parliamentary secretary. I hope that some of the lessons which we learned together in discipline and in working out the problems of national revenue may be of some assistance to him and to you in presiding over what the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) calls this house of minorities.
We are speaking strictly on the amendment which was moved by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacEachen). I am sorry to say that much as I welcome him personally to this house I deplore the fact politically that he happens to be here. But, if we have to have a Liberal from Nova Scotia, there is no one I would rather see here than the hon. member. He will pardon me if I do not propose to comment on the amendment further than was done today by my colleague the Minister of Justice because I am quite sure the hon. member, with his educational background, coming from that province where some people excel in that area, will realize that his arguments were somewhat phony and unrealistic, and that when the Minister of Justice got through with them today he should know there is nothing more I should say about them at this time.
This, Mr. Speaker, is one of the great milestones in the life of a parliament. During our regular sessions of parliament we have this debate on the address which, according to tradition, is always hard fought. It enables hon. members to speak about almost everything under the sun before finally the address is passed and the executive receives the confidence of the house. We are working towards that end at the moment. I am not anticipating what the votes may be, but at least on this occasion we are treading along one of the parliamentary highways which have made great the history of parliamentary procedure within the commonwealth.
334	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Nowlan
As I say, one can speak on almost anything dealing with the affairs of the nation, and in a few moments I shall refer to some of the specific problems with which the Minister of Finance is perhaps more directly associated than any other minister; but I would like to make one or two casual references as I proceed along the way. Recently there has been a great deal of controversy and discussion about the entry of the United Kingdom into the common market. My friend-and I say that advisedly-my friend, the Leader of the Opposition has sometimes spoken caustically about the position that the Prime Minister of Canada has taken with respect to the problems with which this government was confronted in that matter.
Recently the Prime Minister attended the prime ministers' conference in London and, without attempting to read into the record a large number of quotations which one might read because one's time is very limited in this debate, I think it is fair to say that the Leader of the Opposition has criticized the Prime Minister for having taken a position in opposition to the United Kingdom going into the common market, suggesting that he was rather crying about the problems with which we were faced, and altogether belittling the efforts which the Prime Minister was making in defending and protecting the interests of Canada in the event of the possible entry of the United Kingdom into the common market.
This government, of course, has taken the position that it is a problem for the United Kingdom and none other; but I hope the Leader of the Opposition has read the speech made by the Hon. Hugh Gaitskell at the labour conference in Brighton on Wednesday last. One does not have to subscribe to the political tenets of that gentleman-and I do not-to recognize the fact that he is a distinguished leader in the parliament of the United Kingdom and one who some day may possibly be the prime minister of Britain. Although the resolution which was passed by the conference, as of course with all resolutions, had escape valves and escape hatches-and some of us in this parliament are not entirely unfamiliar with that process-certainly the leader of the Labour party came down four square on that occasion in opposition to the United Kingdom going into the common market, because he said it threatened the existence of the commonwealth as such.
We in this party attach a great deal of importance to the common market and to the entry of the United Kingdom into it. We believe it presents problems to us at the moment, but we believe they can be solved. We are also concerned about the future of the commonwealth as such, and I just wonder


if the Leader of the Opposition when he was criticizing the Prime Minister, during those days and weeks when the Prime Minister was overseas, and before and since, knew what he would have the Prime Minister of this country do with the Hon. Hugh Gaitskell, whether he should take the Hon. Hugh Gaitskell by the hair and pull him into the common market or put his shoulder behind him and push him in. But certainly there was a wide divergence of opinion between the two at that time.
With respect to the balance of payments crises which followed after the election, I am not going into the details of that at the moment because we have had a great deal of talk with respect to this, but it has been suggested that the Prime Minister misled the country and deceived the electorate with respect to the position which we took in not going more fully into this matter before the election.
I think the Prime Minister dealt with this matter very effectively the other day, and I am not going to say anything more about it at the moment except to recall the figures which he put before us at that time. I think perhaps I should interpolate this. The Leader of the Opposition I think with a slightly twisted sense of humour, suggested that the reason this crisis developed was because of the lack of confidence in this government. I thought he made that fairly pointed. If that is the case, I would like to ask the Leader of the Opposition how he reconciles the figures, because as the Prime Minister pointed out the other day, between June 1 and June 14 there was a substantial loss in our foreign exchange. There is no question about that.
In fact, there was a loss of $128 million between June 1 and June 14. Then came June 15, which was a Friday, the last day of trading for that week. June 16 was a Saturday; June 17 was a Sunday. Then came June 18. Possibly some people may call that the Black Monday; that was election day. Then you get the balance of exchange for that week. We find that between the 15th and the 22nd, only five trading days, the fund lost $270 million, $142 million more in those five trading days than in the two previous weeks when people in Canada were hoping that this government would still be in power. But when they found that we were in a minority position, when they found that so many Liberals had been elected, there then came a run on foreign exchange control. So, as I say, we lost $142 million more in five days with the dire threat of the hon. gentleman opposite as a possible prime minister than we lost in the two weeks before when the people were hoping the Prime Minister would be returned with his government.

An hon. member opposite says we deceived the electorate, that the Prime Minister deceived the electorate. As I said earlier, the Leader of the Opposition is a good friend of mine, a good personal friend. We happened to come into the House of Commons on the same day more years ago than perhaps we would like to recall. Five of us came in on that day. Only two of us are left. The Leader of the Opposition was then secretary of state for external affairs; he is now the leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. I was a junior backbencher in the House of Commons at that time, and I happen to be standing where I am tonight.
During all these years we have been very, very good friends, and I want to express my appreciation for what the hon. gentleman did when he was a minister and I was a private member. But in view of these misstatements which have been made, the misleading misstatements which have been made with respect to both these matters, and knowing the hon. gentleman as I do, I would hope that before this debate were over he would rise in his place and apologize to this house and the country for the charges he has made.

Perhaps a word should be said with respect to the political complexion of this house. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) said the other night that this is a house of minorities. Naturally our friends in the press gallery are having a lot of fun speculating as to who is supporting who and what machinations or deals are going on behind the scenes. As I think one of the Social Credit party said the other day-at least, he is reported to have said this-perhaps they were a little bit unsophisticated in stating honestly their opinion that this country did not want an election at this time and that it was not the intention of that party to defeat the government for purely political purposes.
This has given a great deal of false courage to our friends on the extreme right and to our friends opposite, each of whom I would
The Address-Mr. Nowlan say are more afraid of an election than I think is the Social Credit party, and they are certainly more afraid of it than we are. So again we see the strange association between the one-time great Liberal party and the socialists now on my right.
The other day the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis)-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.

I am glad to hear that voice. It reminds me of days when we walked up the aisle together confronting the Liberal party when the pipe line debate was on.
However, Mr. Speaker, the other day the hon. member for York South, one of the new members of the House of Commons whose reputation preceded him, in a very able speech expounding socialistic philosophies said, among other things, of this government that we persisted in maintaining a policy of tight money. I will deal with that in a moment, perhaps, if time permits. Then the hon. gentleman continued that the government insisted on reducing expenditures and on chasing that will-o'-the-wisp of a balanced budget willy-nilly, with fingers crossed. A will-o'-the-wisp of a balanced budget-and they went to bed together. Shades of the great Liberal party. It is no wonder that there is some confusion in the gallery above as to who is supporting whom, which deals are made, and why. But in any event, when the division bells ring tonight, because perhaps of the forthrightness, or at least the sincere and honest declarations of our friends of the Social Credit party-I say "our friends" because I am very glad to see people in this house being honest enough to stand up and say what they believe in, instead of hiding behind statements made for their own purposes-or at least when they rang the other night, because far be it from me to say what will happen tonight when the division bells ring-

-the pronounced socialists down on my right and the pseudo-socialists sitting opposite me climbed under the same blanket, shivering and shaking and hoping the lightning would be deflected, because they hoped that the Social Credit party would act as a lightning rod and deflect the lightning so they would not have to face the electorate in the near future. Mr. Speaker, this should be said, and I think it should be said seriously of all party divisions in this house. The government does not agree with the theory of monetary control, the theory of monetary expansion, which is espoused by the Social Credit party. As a matter of fact, I suppose I might say-I hope I will not be

The Address-Mr. Nowlan misunderstood in saying this as Minister of Finance-that it any of us can find any three people in any place in the country who agree on monetary theory, then we are accomplishing a miracle. But be that as it may, we do not think that the theory espoused by the Social Credit party bears this out, but this also should be said. The Social Credit party, according to its pronouncements, stands fairly and squarely on its principle of supporting the maintenance of private enterprise in this country. This government does likewise, Mr. Speaker. In the division which this house saw the other evening you saw a division on principle. You saw parties supporting private enterprise on the one hand, and the socialists and pseudo-socialists divided against them on the other. Mr. Speaker, a very distinguished leader of the Liberal party, the prime minister when I had the opportunity of sitting in this house in opposition, once said that the C.C.F.-at that time there was only the C.C.F. with us-were "Liberals in a hurry". Now I suspect that my hon. friend for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and others who were here in those days when we sat more or less together on the far side of the house, would say that they had witnessed a conversion which was greater than that witnessed by Saul of Tarsus when he was on the road to Damascus, and now we see that it is the Liberals, not the socialists, who are "socialists in a hurry".
Mr. Speaker, having indulged, as I said, in this parliamentary road block when one can cover everything under the sun, and which is one of the great traditions of our parliamentary system, perhaps you would expect me in the very short time which is left to me to deal with some of the financial problems with which we are faced. I trust, Mr. Speaker, that there will be many other opportunities, as 1 am sure there will be if this house has the intelligence which I think it has, for hon. members to raise these points and I will be able to develop further some of the matters which were referred to at this time.
There have been many good speeches made here during this debate. The newspapers have paid tribute, columnists have paid tribute, and I think we all will pay tribute, to the quality of the debate which has taken place so far in this chamber. Not that we agree with all that has been said, but perhaps it does have some merit in having competing groups more closely allied than they were heretofore and you get an expression of views which is refreshing and which is interesting.
The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) is one of the new members of this house whose reputation preceded him as a sort of deus ex machina of the Liberal party, and who I presume can assume to himself some


credit for the rather substantial gains which it made in the last election. He talked the other day about tight money. I could go into this complex subject for a long while, but I am not going to do it at this time. However, I do want to say right now that I deny categorically and absolutely that there is any policy of tight money in this country. The hon. gentleman, as my colleague the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) pointed out the other day, has written at least two books, and he may have to write another one on this matter.
I	am sure he, with his knowledge of economic problems, would be the first to admit, as I know he does, that the needs of our monetary policy must satisfy the needs of our balance of payments position, as well as the needs of our domestic economy. Interest rates did rise. On June 24 the Bank of Canada rate went up to 6 per cent, but on September 7 it was reduced to 5J per cent. Interest rates have eased accordingly.
One could go on and on dealing with the theoretical question of interest rates, but the interest rate of the bank itself is not the only criterion by which this government should be judged. It is not the only criterion by which the people of this country are going to judge this government when the time comes.
There are various mechanisms which we have to which I think some attention should be paid. Let us take the industrial development bank, for instance, for the moment. We talk of tight money. The loans in 1961 amounted to $71 million, which is 85 per cent more than in 1960. You could go down through the various classifications covered. In the retail trade you find that loans were up 150 per cent. Loans to the construction industry increased by 140 per cent. Manufacturing loans in some fields were up over 100 per cent- over 200 per cent in some cases-and in the
II	months of this year, and we are not through this year yet, including the period of the alleged austerity program-and I would like to take half an hour on that, but time does not permit-they are up over 31 per cent. The loans issued by the industrial development bank are up 31 per cent over last year at this time. If that is tight money, Mr. Speaker, then give us more of it.
Then let us take the loans under the Farm Credit Act. In the fiscal year ending March 31, 1962, loans totalled $68.6 million, an increase of $8 million over 1960. In the first six months of this year there has been an increase of 22 per cent over the loans made in the same period last year.
Let us take the Small Businesses Loans Act, which, Mr. Speaker, you and I have good reason to know, having worked on the bill in days gone by. Loans up to December 31, 1961 totalled $25.6 million, and they were

made to various classes of business. Loans for the second quarter of this year are running at an annual rate 21 per cent over last year. Mr. Speaker, is that tight money? With regard to home improvement loans, in 1961 they rose to a record level of $42.8 million compared to $30 million the year before. For the first seven months of this year the report of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation shows although the figures are not definite and conclusive, a definite improvement and an increase in loans over the same period last year. And one could go on.
Those are the principal lending agencies which this government is operating and which are being developed, and have been developed, under the aegis of this government. Then, of course, you have the Export Credits Insurance Act, amendments to which are being brought forward in the near future. I am not sure what business has been set forth for the rest of the week, but I think very shortly the house will be asked to deal with those matters. Section 21, the long term credit section which provides for exports of our products to the world, was absolutely inoperative under the preceding administration. Under this government we have loaned $100 million, almost $200 million, and we are going to ask for an increase of that amount so that we can continue our export sales program which has been instituted and carried on so well by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees). And that is only one measure, Mr. Speaker.
I am warned that my time is running very short, Mr. Speaker, but I might also mention the substantial purchase of bonds which has taken place, and I am sure the hon. member for Davenport will appreciate that. A large number of bonds have been sold in the last few months following the problems that we faced. The bonds have all been taken up on the domestic market, and that of itself shows the confidence of the Canadian people in government bonds. Hundreds of millions of dollars have been made available from the banking system. I am not saying at the moment what tight money is. At the moment I am not trying to define what the level of the currency should be in this nation. That is a matter for determination and for government policy from time to time. However, I say this without hesitation or without fear. If the policy which this government is following is that of tight money, then Mr. Scrooge who is referred to by Dickens in his work, was a Santa Claus. There can be no question whatsoever about that matter. I think we have proven fairly well that substantial funds are available for various media of employment and development in this country. Having said all those things, and there are many more
The Address-Mr. Pearson that I could say but my time is running very rapidly to an end, I do not wish anyone to assume for one minute that we feel we have solved all the problems of this country. There are many difficult problems ahead of us, including the balance of payments problem with respect to the over $1 billion a year that we pay out for services, dividends, interest and goods. Only once in the last 10 years under the aegis of this government have we had a surplus of goods, and that was last year.

I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, whether this is a scientific problem which you are trying to overcome-

If I venture to intervene in this debate, Mr. Speaker, it is because of the

The Address~Mr. Pearson extremely friendly invitation or indeed challenge, issued to me by the Minister of Finance a moment ago. An invitation or challenge, if you like, couched in such friendly terms by one whom I admire personally so much is one that I think I should not turn down. This also gives me an opportunity to congratulate the minister on his new portfolio. I rejoice in his steady promotion on the ministerial ladder as a member of the class of '48. I thank him for his friendly references to myself and I most warmly reciprocate them as he knows.
The Minister of Finance spoke for one half hour and when he had ten minutes left he said, "It is time now for me to deal with finance". The minister should be more careful to speak as Minister of Finance at every opportunity. In this debate this is the first time we have heard from the Minister of Finance when so many financial subjects were being discussed and dealt with on the other side by the former minister of finance, now the Minister of Justice, who is still minister of finance so far as international financial affairs seem to be concerned and who is still the Canadian member of the international monetary fund and the bank of international settlements. I therefore suggest in a friendly way to the Minister of Finance that he take every opportunity to prove that he is the Minister of Finance, especially as there seems to be lurking in the other house someone who has aspirations in that field as well. We do not wish to see our old friend the Minister of Finance crushed between the upper and the lower millstones.
I am delighted that the minister has kept his sense of humour, which has stood him in such good stead over the years and which I hope will do so in the future. Perhaps he has never given a better illustration of his possession of that sense of humour than he has given tonight in the remarks which he has just made, especially when he said that we have nothing like tight money in this country at the present time. Then he went on to say, however, that he was not quite sure what tight money was, that he was not going to define it tonight. But whatever it is, we have not got it.
I ask him to inquire of any small businessman who is trying to get a loan whether we have tight money. I ask him to go to a bank and try to arrange a small overdraft and to find out whether we have tight money. The minister will no doubt on some other occasion tell us what he means by tight money. However, I tell him tonight that we certainly have tight money in this country at the present time.


Another example of the minister's sense of humour was given when he invited me to rise in my place at once in this debate before it was brought to a conclusion on this amendment and apologize.

If any apology is due to this house, Mr. Speaker, it is due from the other side. I do not accept the minister's invitation on this occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I will repeat it later on.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The minister said, "Our attitude toward the common market and Great Britain's entry into the common market must have been right because it was supported by the leader of the Labour party in Great Britain". He asked me whether I had read Mr. Gaitskell's statement. Of course I have read it. I have also read Mr. Macmillan's statement on the same subject. Our criticism of the government in this matter is a simple one. It is not that they are not trying to protect Canadian interests, and I hope I made this position clear in my first speech.
The criticism is that they do not know how to protect Canadian interests; and that in their efforts to protect Canadian interests, by adopting a shortsighted, narrow minded policy they have made Canada's reputation in this particular field lower than it should have been. Our criticism is that they have no understanding of the implications of this great move of Great Britain across the channel in the interests of the political and economic unification of Europe and the Atlantic world, something that may stand between us and destruction in the years ahead. We can have that and the commonwealth too, Mr. Speaker, but hon. gentlemen opposite do not seem to understand that fact.
The other subject for apology is the concealment of the financial facts during the election. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan) proved how right they were and how wrong we were and that they had concealed nothing because there was no crisis until two days after the election. That was the argument. He brought forward the figures that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) had brought forward before to show that we had lost, how much, in those two days? One hundred and

The Address-Mr. Pearson
eighty million dollars or $200 million in a couple of days. According to him, and this is a magnificent example of the minister's sense of humour, the reason for that loss of dollars which reflected lack of confidence was that the people, presumably in Canada and outside of Canada, who are concerned with these international financial transactions had suddenly realized that the Liberals had elected 100 members in the new house. The reason for it, Mr. Speaker, is that the people who are concerned in these matters suddenly realized that the Liberals had not elected enough to take charge of the government at once.
The morning after the election, Mr. Speaker, the international and the national financial communities suddenly realized that this government had not been replaced, and on that knowledge dollars fled the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You have the sense of humour.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance had something to say about the amendment on which we are voting in a few moments. It is a very simple one, Mr. Speaker. It condemns the government for taxation without representation. It is a historic and age-old principle of British constitutional law and propriety that there shall be no taxes levied on the people without the people's representatives having a chance to express their will in respect of such taxes.
What have we got now? We have a government that has put into effect taxation by order in council. We on this side challenge the legality of that order in council. That is a matter for legal dispute. They say it is legal; but saying it is legal does not necessarily make it legal. Even if you assume it is legal, even if you assume that there is a legal basis for this action, the government having taken the action now refuses to give the people's representatives a chance to pass on the action they took by order in council.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Nonsense. That is what we are going to do right now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is the issue. The Minister of Justice says that we are doing it now because we are voting on a motion of confidence in the speech from the throne. In this motion is that particular action of the government under consideration? Is it to be decided on any motion of confidence? The Minister of Justice knows it is a fantastic argument that if we vote the address in reply to the speech from the throne we confirm and ratify all the actions of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You have raised it yourself in this amendment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: But, Mr. Speaker, taxation without representation and refusing to let the representatives of the people even discuss the matter-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is perfectly ridiculous.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: -that is what is being done now. The Minister of Justice tries to support this, the Minister of Justice who once draped himself in a Canadian flag and walked out of this house because he said parliament's and the people's rights were being debased.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They were too. You were a party to that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I ask the Prime Minister once again, as the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) did this afternoon, is he going to give this parliament a chance to decide and to express its opinion on the austerity program of the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You have been doing it for ten days now.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: There is going to be no opportunity given for us to discuss and decide on the taxation measures put into effect by the government by order in council and covering over $200 million of the people's money. That is the position that the government has taken. That is the issue in the amendment. It is as simple as that. We condemn the government. We have no confidence in a government that will take action of that kind, taxation on the basis of very doubtful legality at best, and then refusal to let the representatives of the people even discuss what they, the government, have done. How can any member of this House of Commons-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What have you been doing all these days?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: -who believes in parliamentary government vote against an amendment of this kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What have you been doing for the past two weeks?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We put this subamendment before the house confident that every member of the house who really believes in parliamentary rights, parliamentary privileges and parliamentary government will vote for it and, Mr. Speaker, if the subamendment carries, if it means a general election, who are we to run away from a general election at this time?
It is very hard indeed, Mr. Speaker, to understand that a government, headed by my right hon. friend who once talked so much about the rights and privileges of parliament, will come into this house and tell us: We have done this by order in council and that

Division
is the last you are going to hear about it; you will be given no chance even to discuss it, let alone decide on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You have been doing it for two weeks.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is the very negation of parliamentary government-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: This is a negation of the facts.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: -and that is only one reason why we have no confidence of any kind in this minority government at this time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am informed that it is 9.30, Mr. Speaker, and the vote is to be taken at 9.30. Therefore-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order. It being 9.30 o'clock p.m., it is my duty, pursuant to section 4 of standing order 38, to interrupt these proceedings and put forthwith the question on any amendment or amendments before the house.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I declare the amendment lost.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It now being ten o'clock this house stands adjourned until 2.30 o'clock tomorrow afternoon.
At ten o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

Wednesday, October 10, 1962
